title: Two minutes against the clock
objectives: Combine every method in a timed round and track your score.
Choose a division method at a glance from the size of the answer and the divisor

screens.title: Two minutes against the clock
screens.prose: A Zetamac round gives you 120 seconds of mixed questions. We will set a pace, sort each division by the method it needs, then race a round of ten.
Your target is a score of 30: thirty correct answers in 120 seconds. Steady pacing spreads them evenly across the round.
screens.question: Drag the point to the time your 10th answer should be in.

hints.text: How many seconds does each answer get?
$120 \div 30 = 4$ seconds an answer.
Ten answers at 4 seconds each take 40 seconds.

feedback.correct: Four seconds an answer, so ten answers take 40 seconds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the seconds per answer, then multiply by 10.

byKey.count: You placed the point at 10 seconds, the answer count. The line measures time.
byKey.per-ten: 12 seconds is $120 \div 10$, the pace for a score of 10. You want 30 answers.
byKey.quarter: 30 seconds is a quarter of the round. Ten of thirty answers is a third of it.

explain.text: Thirty answers in 120 seconds is $120 \div 30 = 4$ seconds each. Ten answers take $10 \times 4 = 40$ seconds, a third of the round.

screens.prose: Drag the point to set the seconds you spend on each answer. The caption shows the score that pace gives over 120 seconds.

derive.caption: {{fixed(s.x, 1)}} seconds an answer gives a score of {{floor(120 / s.x)}}

screens.question: How many seconds an answer gives a score of 40?

hints.text: Forty answers share 120 seconds.
Drag the point until the caption says 40.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share the 120 seconds among 40 answers.

byKey.thirty: 4 seconds an answer gives 30. A score of 40 needs a faster pace.
byKey.flipped: $\tfrac13$ is answers per second. The question asks for seconds per answer.
byKey.gap: 80 is the gap between 40 and 120. Divide the time by the answers instead.

explain.text: Forty answers in 120 seconds leaves $120 \div 40 = 3$ seconds each. Each second you save per answer adds a lot of score at the fast end.

screens.prose: Seconds per answer is your **pace**: $\text{pace} = 120 \div \text{score}$. Pace leaks on questions you cannot recall. So sort each division before you start it.
screens.question: Tap every division whose answer is bigger than 12, past the times table.

hints.text: For each one, ask: is the answer more than 12?
Multiply the divisor by 12. If the number is bigger, the answer is past the table.
$4 \times 12 = 48 < 96$, $5 \times 12 = 60 < 135$ and $8 \times 12 = 96 < 176$. The others are table facts.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each number with the divisor times 12.

byKey.r0c1: $84 \div 7 = 12$, the last row of the table. Recall it.
byKey.r3c1: You missed $135 \div 5$. Since $5 \times 12 = 60$, the answer is past the table.
byKey.r5c1: You missed $176 \div 8$. Since $8 \times 12 = 96$, the answer is past the table.

explain.text: You compared each number with the divisor times 12. Questions 1 and 5 land exactly on 12, so they are still recall. The other three need a method: halving, doubling or splitting.

screens.prose: Here is the method card from this level. Each division below is labelled with its method. Work them in order.

rows: Split at multiples of the divisor

screens.question: Fill in each answer.

hints.text: Use the method in each row, not a new one.
168 halves to 84, then 42, then 21.
12, then 48 to 24, then 230 to 23, then 21, then $10 + 3 = 13$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows with the method in their row.

explain.text: Each method took two or three quick steps. The card tells you which one to reach for, so no time goes on choosing. Next, the same round without the labels.

screens.prose: Now a round of ten with no labels. Choose each method from the card. A score of 25 means about 48 seconds for ten, so time yourself.

rows: Split at multiples of the divisor

screens.question: Fill in all ten answers.

hints.text: Sort first: which ones can you recall?
Recall 63 ÷ 9, 132 ÷ 12 and 88 ÷ 11. Halve for ÷ 4 and ÷ 8. Double for ÷ 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the amber rows with the method from the card.

explain.text: Three were recall, two halvings, two doublings and three splits. Sorting took a glance, and each method took two or three steps. That is how a round stays near 4.8 seconds an answer.

screens.prose: Tracking scores shows whether practice is working. One round is noisy, so average the week. Here are five daily scores.
screens.question: What is the average score for the week?

hints.text: Add the five scores, then divide by 5.
The scores add to 105.
$105 \div 5$: double to 210, then divide by 10. That is 21.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the scores, then divide by how many there are.

byKey.sum: 105 is the total. Divide it by the 5 days.
byKey.best: 24 is the best day. The average uses every day.
byKey.last: 23 is Friday alone. The average uses every day.

explain.text: The five scores add to 105. Dividing by 5 is doubling then dividing by 10: $210 \div 10 = 21$. Thursday and Friday are above the average, a sign of progress.

screens.prose: Under the clock, a quick split cuts at a round number. Try $126 \div 7$ split as $100 + 26$. The rectangle is 7 tall.
screens.question: Which split of $126 \div 7$ finishes in one step per piece?

options.why: You split at a hundred. $100 \div 7$ is 14 remainder 2, so both pieces stall.
You split off the tens. $120 \div 7$ and $6 \div 7$ both leave remainders.
That splits the divisor 7. Only the number being divided can be split.

hints.text: Which multiple of 7 is close to 126?
$7 \times 10 = 70$. What is left after taking 70 from 126?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split 126 into two multiples of 7.

byKey.hundred: You split at a hundred. $100 \div 7$ is 14 remainder 2, so both pieces stall.

explain.text: Splitting at 100 left remainders in both pieces: 14 r 2 and 3 r 5. Split at multiples of 7 instead. Then $70 + 56$ gives $10 + 8 = 18$, and $18 \times 7 = 126$.

screens.prose: Here is the triage you used. Recall when the answer is in the table. Halve for $\div 4$ and $\div 8$. Double, then divide by 10, for $\div 5$. Otherwise split at multiples of the divisor: $$a \div b = (mb + nb) \div b = m + n$$
screens.question: Use it on $232 \div 8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dividing by 8 is three halvings.

byKey.two-halvings: 58 is two halvings, which divides by 4. Halve once more.
byKey.one-halving: 116 is one halving. Dividing by 8 needs three.

explain.text: The divisor is 8, so the card says halve three times: 116, 58, 29. Check: $29 \times 8 = 232$.

screens.prose: Write out the split for $204 \div 12$, one justified step per line.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

hints.text: What has to happen before any dividing?
The split of 204 comes first. Then each piece is divided.
Split, divide each piece, recall the facts, add.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the 204 first, then divide each piece by 12.

explain.text: The split comes first because it decides the pieces. Each piece is then a table fact: $120 \div 12 = 10$ and $84 \div 12 = 7$. Adding gives 17.

screens.prose: On a desk, the same skills run against a different clock. Here is a round of four quick checks from a trading day.
screens.question: Fill in the four answers.

rows: A £9.60 fee on a £3,200.00 trade, as a decimal
£1,500.00 profit on £12,000.00 capital, as a decimal
The 40% bond sleeve of a £7,250.00 book (£)

hints.text: Each row uses one method from this level.
Price: 1,182 is 1,200 take away 18. Fee: 1% of £3,200 is £32.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the amber rows one method at a time.

byKey.r1c1: 1% of £3,200 is £32, so £9.60 is 0.3%. As a decimal that is 0.003.

explain.text: The price split $1182$ as $1200 - 18$, giving $100 - 1.5 = 98.5$. The fee is 0.3% of the trade and the return is $\tfrac18$. The bond sleeve is four lots of £725.

ideas: Pace is seconds per answer: $120 \div \text{score}$. A score of 30 needs 4 seconds an answer.
Sort before you work: recall table facts, halve for 4 and 8, double for 5, and split the rest.
Split at multiples of the divisor, not at round numbers: 126 is 70 + 56 for 7.

formula.name: Splitting at multiples
formula.tex: a \div b = (mb + nb) \div b = m + n
formula.note: Choose $mb$ and $nb$ as multiples of $b$ that you know.

summary.trap: Splitting $126 \div 7$ as $100 + 26$ leaves remainders in both pieces. Split as $70 + 56$.

quiz.question: What was your pace, in seconds per answer?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the time by the score.

byKey.flipped: 0.25 is answers per second, $30 \div 120$. Pace is seconds per answer.
byKey.gap: 90 is 120 take away 30. Divide the time by the score.

explain.text: Pace is time divided by score: $120 \div 30 = 4$ seconds an answer.

quiz.prose: Past the table, split at multiples of the divisor.
quiz.question: What is $196 \div 7$?

explain.text: $196 = 140 + 56$, both multiples of 7. That gives $20 + 8 = 28$. Check: $28 \times 7 = 196$.

quiz.question: What is the best first move?

options.why: Neither 100 nor 17 is a multiple of 9, so both pieces leave remainders.
Halving divides by 2, 4 or 8. Nine is odd, and 117 halves to 58.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the method on the card that suits 9.

explain.text: Nine is not 4, 5 or 8, so split at multiples of 9: $117 = 90 + 27$. That gives $10 + 3 = 13$.

quiz.prose: Your scores over five days were 22, 25, 24, 27 and 27.
quiz.question: What is your average?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the five scores, then divide by 5.

byKey.sum: 125 is the total. Divide by the 5 days.
